pageInfo.subtitle: Break out of isolated boxes, master smooth position shifting, guide-finger slides, and connect the entire neck horizontally.
pageInfo.heroDescription: The single most common barrier preventing guitarists from reaching true creative freedom is the 'box trap'—getting stuck in isolated, vertical scale shapes and feeling lost when trying to move up or down the neck. The guitar fretboard is not a collection of fragmented boxes, but an interconnected geometric matrix. By mastering guide-finger sliding, octave shortcuts, single-string horizontal highways, and CAGED anchor positions, you learn to navigate all 24 frets with the effortless spatial intuition of a concert pianist.

items.text: The Sliding Thumb Anchor: Never clamp your thumb in place while the fingers reach for distant frets. The thumb must glide smoothly along the spine of the neck as an integrated unit with the palm.

Guide Finger Rails: When shifting positions along a string, keep the fretting finger in light physical contact with the string as a sensory guide rail rather than lifting it completely off into space.
The Micro-Release Principle: Release 90% of fretting pressure the millisecond before shifting, allowing your fingers to skate across the fret tops effortlessly without string squeak.
Eyes Before Fingers: Train your eyes to target the destination fret marker a split-second before your fretting hand initiates the shift; your hand will land with laser accuracy.
Blindfolded Tactile Calibration: Practice shifting between frets 5 and 12 with your eyes closed, relying purely on muscle memory and the tactile sensation of fret spacing.
The Octave Matrix: Internalize the universal octave shapes: down 2 frets and up 2 strings (strings 6->4 and 5->3), and down 3 frets and up 2 strings across the B string (strings 4->2 and 3->1).
The B-String Tuning Compensation: Because the B string is tuned to a major third instead of a fourth, all octave and chord shapes shift up by one fret when crossing onto string 2.
Single-String Linear Visualization: Practice playing entire scales along a single string to understand musical intervals (half steps and whole steps) linearly like a piano keyboard.
Unison Pitch Recognition: Learn where identical pitches exist on adjacent strings (e.g., 5th fret high E is the exact same pitch as 10th fret B string) for tone color variation.
CAGED Root Triangulation: Connect every scale and chord back to its root note on strings 6, 5, or 4 to instantly orient yourself in any key across any fret.

exercises.title: Single-String Chromatic Position Shifting (String 1)
exercises.description: Develop smooth, gliding hand movement. Play a 1-2-3-4 pattern on the high E string, shift up one fret to play 2-3-4-5, and continue ascending the neck. Focus on shifting the hand as a single unified vehicle.

patternNote.text: Movement: Horizontal chromatic climbing with unified hand-and-thumb glide

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Keep your thumb gliding along the back of the neck in exact synchronization with the fretting hand. The shift should be decisive and smooth without stopping the beat.

exercises.title: The Universal Octave Matrix Across All String Pairs
exercises.description: Master the master key of fretboard mapping: octave shapes. Play root-octave pairs between strings 6 & 4, 5 & 3, 4 & 2, and 3 & 1. Notice the shape shift across the B string offset.

patternNote.text: Matrix: Strings 6->4 & 5->3 (+2 frets) vs. Strings 4->2 & 3->1 (+3 frets)

notation.title: Universal Octave Matrix Across String Pairs

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Say the note names aloud as you play: 'G, G, C, C, G, G, C, C'. This embeds octave recognition into your subconscious, allowing you to instantly double any solo line in octaves like Wes Montgomery.

exercises.title: Horizontal Single-String Major Scale (C Major on String 2)
exercises.description: Ditch vertical box thinking by playing the complete C major scale horizontally along the B string from the 1st fret (C) to the 13th fret (high C). This visualizes whole and half steps linearly.

notation.title: Horizontal C Major Scale on the B String

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Use fingers 1 and 3 for whole-step shifts and finger 1 to 2 for half-step shifts. Notice the half steps between E-F (frets 5-6) and B-C (frets 12-13).

exercises.title: Guide-Finger Sliding Drill: Pentatonic Shift Highway
exercises.description: Connect Pentatonic Box 1 to Box 2 using finger 3 as a guide rail. Slide smoothly from fret 7 to fret 9 on the G string, opening up the entire upper register without missing a beat.

patternNote.text: Technique: Guide finger slide on G string connecting Box 1 (fret 5) and Box 2 (fret 8)

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: In measure 1, slide finger 3 from fret 7 to fret 9. Maintain light contact with the string during the slide—do not lift your finger off and try to hop into position.

sections.title: Advanced Fluency: CAGED Highway & Multi-Octave Arpeggios

exercises.title: The Diagonal 3-Octave Pentatonic Highway
exercises.description: Traverse the entire fretboard in a single diagonal sprint from fret 5 on the low E string to fret 17 on the high E string. This links three distinct pentatonic boxes into one unified melodic highway.

patternNote.text: Highway: 3-octave A minor pentatonic run climbing diagonally across 12 frets

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Shift positions on the string crossings: shift during the move from string 5 to 4, and again from string 3 to 2. The diagonal trajectory creates explosive velocity with minimal finger strain.

exercises.title: Unison Note Calibration Across Adjacent Strings
exercises.description: Every note on the guitar (except the lowest 4 notes) can be played in multiple locations. This exercise drills unison notes across adjacent strings, training you to hear how timbre changes from thick wound strings to bright plain strings.

patternNote.text: Concept: Identical pitch played on high E (fret 5) and B (fret 10)

notation.title: Unison Note Matching Across Adjacent Strings

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Notice how the 10th fret on the B string has a warmer, woodier timbre than the 5th fret on the high E string, even though the pitch (A 440Hz) is acoustically identical.

exercises.title: The Full CAGED Arpeggio Traversal (C Major Across 5 Positions)
exercises.description: The ultimate test of fretboard vision: outline C major arpeggios seamlessly across all 5 CAGED positions—C-shape (open), A-shape (fret 3), G-shape (fret 5), E-shape (fret 8), and D-shape (fret 10)—in a continuous ascending cascade.

patternNote.text: Master Run: C major arpeggio connecting all 5 CAGED positions up to fret 12

notation.title: Full CAGED C Major Arpeggio Neck Traversal

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Visualize the chord shape before your fingers touch the strings. This exercise permanently unifies the fretboard into one continuous harmonic landscape.

items.title: 3 Mistakes That Keep You Trapped in Boxes
items: The 'Box 1' Pentatonic Prison: Only learning vertical scale patterns. If you only move across strings in one 4-fret span, you will never feel comfortable traveling horizontally along the neck.
Stiff Thumb Anchoring During Shifts: Leaving the thumb glued behind fret 5 while reaching your fingers up to fret 9. The thumb and fretting hand must slide together as an integrated carriage.
Hopping Instead of Sliding: Lifting fingers entirely off the strings during position shifts. Using guide fingers on string rails keeps your hand oriented and eliminates wrong-fret landings.

items.title: Masters of Fretboard Fluency
items: Pat Metheny: Modern jazz giant who visualizes the fretboard in horizontal intervals, fluidly sliding across positions to create singing, horn-like chromatic runs.
Guthrie Govan: Modern virtuoso renowned for complete fretboard mastery; can play any scale, mode, or chord inversion anywhere on the neck without pausing.
Allan Holdsworth: Legendary fusion pioneer who mapped the neck in symmetric 4-note-per-string patterns, bypassing conventional boxes entirely.
Joe Pass: Bebop solo guitar master who navigated chord melodies across all 12 positions using root octave anchors and chromatic guide tones.

items.title: The 10-Minute Daily Fretboard Navigation Routine
items: Block 1: Single-String Horizontal Scale & Chromatics (3 min) - Run Exercises 1 & 3 along the B and high E strings at 70–75 BPM, naming scale intervals as you shift.
Block 2: Universal Octave Matrix (3 min) - Cycle all octave pairs across all 6 strings at 75 BPM, calling note names aloud to cement visual landmarks.
Block 3: Diagonal Pentatonic Highway & CAGED (4 min) - Sprint through Exercises 5 & 7 at 85 BPM, sliding smoothly through all 5 positions.
